source_text: Postquam parabolae illius vanitate reprehensa sanxit sententiam promulgatione atque obtestatione divina, etiam iustitiae suae dignatur aperire rationem, cur necessitudines peccatis non graventur alternis. Quoniam omnes animae - inquit - meae sunt, quemadmodum anima patris, ita et anima filii; omnes animae meae sunt; anima, quae peccat, ipsa morietur [n58] . Quare ergo esset aequissima sententiae ista moderatio, proprietate quoque ostendit animarum.
pass_a_gloss: After the vanity of that parable has been reprehended he has sanctioned the sentence by a divine promulgation and obtestation; he also deigns to open the account of his justice, why kinships are not burdened by alternating sins. Since all souls, he says, are mine, as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son; all souls are mine; the soul which sins, itself will die. Why therefore this moderation of the sentence would be most fair, he also shows by the property of souls.

lemmas.lexica: LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS ratio; Blaise use of reason required for sin
LS anima; Blaise human soul as image

pass_b_english: After exposing the emptiness of that proverb and ratifying his judgment by a divine declaration and oath, he also deigns to explain the reason for his justice: why relatives are not burdened with each other’s sins. ‘All souls are mine,’ he says; ‘the father’s soul and the son’s soul alike—all souls are mine. The soul that sins shall itself die’ (Ezekiel 18:4). Thus he also uses his ownership of souls to show why this measured judgment is perfectly fair.

choices.why: Julian's forensic virtue that renders to each his own, without fraude or gratia (partiality).
rejected: righteousness (Pauline overlay unless the verse forces it)

choices.why: For Julian, sin requires rational choice; infants lack usus rationis.
